t: Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020
a: Ministry of Labour & Employment (MoLE); Inspector-cum-Facilitator (ICF) at state/central level
sum: The primary workplace-safety statute in India. In force from 21 Nov 2025; it repealed 13 central Acts including the Factories Act 1948, BOCW Act 1996, Contract Labour Act 1970, Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979, Mines Act 1952 and Dock Workers Act 1986. Applies to establishments with 10+ workers (all establishments carrying hazardous activity regardless of headcount).
key: s.3 – single registration of establishment (60 days of applicability); existing registrants update details via Shram Suvidha (Central Rules: Form I, within 6 months of 8 May 2026)
s.6 – general duties of employer: safe workplace, plant, systems, information, annual health examination (as prescribed)
s.10 – notice of accident (death or injury) to ICF; s.11 – dangerous occurrences (even without injury); s.12 – notice of notifiable diseases

s.16–s.22 – National & State OSH Advisory Boards; s.22 Safety Committee (threshold as prescribed, e.g. 500+ workers; hazardous-process factories lower); s.23 Safety Officer (factory 500+, hazardous factory 250+, construction 250+, mine 100+ — verify thresholds in applicable rules)
s.24 – welfare: canteen (100+), crèche (50+), first-aid, drinking water, latrines, welfare officer (250+)
s.25–s.27 – working hours (8 h/day), overtime at twice ordinary wage, rest intervals; s.43 women may work at night with consent and safeguards

Ch. XI – contract labour (threshold 50+); Ch. XII – hazardous processes (compulsory disclosure, safety report, emergency plan, exposure limits); Ch. XIII – building and other construction work; Part on mines
Registers, annual return (unified), inspection by ICF with web-based randomised inspection; graded penalties with compounding; employer may be prosecuted on second offence
note: Labour is a concurrent subject: Central Rules apply where the Central Government is the appropriate Government; otherwise the State's OSH Rules apply. During transition, state Factories/BOCW Rules continue to be used where state OSH rules are not yet final.

t: Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (Central) Rules, 2026
sum: Operational rules under the OSH Code for Central-sphere establishments (railways, mines, major ports, oilfields, central PSUs, etc.). Also the model many states are following for their own rules.
key: Registration: Form I (online), certificate in Form III within 7 days; register of establishments in Form V

Rule 7 – Notice of accidents & dangerous occurrences: death – forthwith (electronic + written; inform police and family); injury preventing work 48 h or more and listed dangerous occurrences – within 12 h, Form XI, to ICF and District Magistrate/SDO

Schedule of dangerous occurrences: collapse of lifting machine/crane/hoist, explosion/fire causing damage, bursting of pressure vessel, collapse of structure/scaffold, electrical short-circuit/fire, release of hazardous substance, etc.
Hours of work: 8 h/day, 48 h/week; spread-over; overtime cap per quarter; women night work conditions (transport, CCTV, lighting, batch size)
Health examination, Safety Committee constitution & functions, Safety Officer qualifications, welfare standards, contract labour licence (5-year all-India licence)
note: Where a State Government is the appropriate Government (most private factories and construction sites in Karnataka/Tamil Nadu), use the State OSH Rules; until those are final, the legacy State Factories Rules and BOCW Rules remain the working technical standard.

t: Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, 2023 (as amended) – Indian Carbon Market (ICM)
a: BEE (administrator); Ministry of Power; CPCB (compensation); Grid Controller of India (registry); CERC (trading on power exchanges)
sum: India's compliance carbon market. GHG emission intensity (GEI) targets notified under the EC Act for obligated entities: aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp & paper (8 Oct 2025, 282 plants) and petroleum refineries, petrochemicals, textiles (16 Jan 2026) — 490 entities in 7 sectors; iron & steel targets issued as a draft (G.S.R. 517(E), 26 June 2026, 255 units) and fertilizer still pending. Targets apply to FY2025-26 and FY2026-27 against a FY2023-24 baseline (about 40% of the reduction due in year one). Over-performers receive Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs) to sell; under-performers must buy and surrender CCCs; an offset mechanism lets non-obligated entities register projects.
key: Obligated entity: monitoring plan approved by BEE; monthly monitoring; verified GHG emission report by an Accredited Carbon Verification Agency (ACVA) within 4 months of FY end (FY2025-26 → 31 Jul 2026; FY2026-27 → 31 Jul 2027)
CCC issuance on the ICM registry (BEE procedure date 30 Sep 2026 for the first cycle); trading only on CERC-registered power exchanges (first trades expected late 2026)
Shortfall: buy CCCs; failing that, environmental compensation by CPCB equal to twice the average CCC price of the cycle; shortfall recorded
Scope 2 for CCTS uses the CEA grid emission factor (CO2 Baseline Database v20: 0.727 tCO2/MWh for FY2023-24 weighted average; check v21)
Links to BRSR (Principle 6 disclosures) and to EU CBAM (verified installation data reusable)
note: Sector coverage, baselines and deadlines change by notification — the statement above reflects reporting up to early Oct 2026; confirm the current GEI notification for your sector.

t: EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) – Regulation (EU) 2023/956 as amended by (EU) 2025/2083
a: European Commission; EU national competent authorities; authorised CBAM declarants (EU importers)
sum: Definitive regime from 1 Jan 2026 for cement, iron & steel (incl. listed downstream articles), aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen. EU importers must be authorised declarants and will buy CBAM certificates priced on EU ETS auctions (certificate sales open 1 Feb 2027; first annual declaration and surrender for 2026 imports due 30 Sep 2027). De minimis: importers at or below 50 t/yr of the goods (not electricity/hydrogen) are exempt. Indian exporters feel it through buyer demands for installation-level verified emissions data; default values carry mark-ups (10% in 2026, 20% in 2027, 30% from 2028). A carbon price effectively paid in India (e.g. CCTS) may be deductible for actual-data declarations once the Commission's rules are final.
key: Exporter actions: map products to CN codes; set up installation-level MRV (direct + indirect emissions, precursors); third-party verification; register installation in the CBAM registry; supply data to EU customers; compare default vs verified cost
Overlaps: CCTS verified reports, ISO 14064, GHG Protocol; free allocation deduction shrinks to 2034
